title: Rainy Day Story Quest Pack
audience: Parents, homeschool families, tutors, and elementary teachers working with reluctant writers ages 7-11.
safetyNote: No scary harm, no bullying, no romance, no weapons, no branded characters, no real child profiles.

cover.headline: Rainy Day Story Quest Pack
cover.subhead: Four tiny weather worlds help kids map, speak, describe, build sentences, choose a kind ending, and finish one short story without staring at a blank page.
included: Rainy-day route map with dry-path choices
Tiny forecast cards for Teacup Town
Parent and teacher guide for a 35-minute writing session

setup: Print the pack single-sided so kids can spread pages out and point before writing.
Choose one pencil, one crayon or highlighter, and one quiet spot near a window if possible.
Keep the session offline with no accounts, no uploads, and no public sharing.
Let the child skip one page and return to it after the final story draft.

sessionFlow.title: Pick the world
sessionFlow.instruction: Read the cover and let the child choose the first world by pointing, circling, or saying the title aloud.

sessionFlow.title: Map the route
sessionFlow.instruction: Use the route map to choose where the hero starts, stops, and notices one weather clue.

sessionFlow.title: Gather words
sessionFlow.instruction: Complete the forecast, description, dialogue, or sentence page before asking for full paragraphs.

sessionFlow.title: Draft the story
sessionFlow.instruction: Move selected words and sentences onto the final story page in beginning, middle, and ending order.

sessionFlow.title: Share and revise
sessionFlow.instruction: Ask the child to read one favorite sentence and add one clearer detail, label, or speech line.

supportMoves: Offer two choices instead of asking an open question when the child gets stuck.
Let the child draw or label first, then turn one label into a sentence together.
Write down the child's spoken sentence exactly once, then ask them to copy or improve one word.
Use a timer for a short writing burst, but stop before the page feels crowded.
Praise a concrete move such as a clear clue, polite dialogue line, or useful map label.
extensionIdeas: Turn the forecast cards into a second story set on a sunny day.
Use a measuring cup or real rain gauge to add one true weather note.
Let two children write different endings from the same map.
Staple the final story behind the favorite planning page for a small portfolio piece.

pages.title: Start Here: Rainy Day Quest
pages.kidDirection: Circle one world you want to visit first.
pages.adultNote: Use this overview to make the session feel small and choice-based.

sections.heading: Choose a Quest World
lines: Teacup Town Weather Window: forecast clues in a tiny teacup.
Rain Gauge Railway: water samples, garden posts, and train switches.
Spoon Ferry Lunchbox Harbor: snack orders and polite dock talk.
Rain Boot Route Rangers: puddle maps and dry delivery paths.

pages.title: Adult Guide: 35-Minute Session
pages.kidDirection: Ask your adult to read the first step aloud.
pages.adultNote: Run the pages as short stations, not as a test.

sections.heading: When Writing Slows Down
lines: Offer: draw it, label it, or say it first.
Prompt: Which clue helps the hero next?
Prompt: What would the helper say politely?

pages.title: Rain Boot Route Map
pages.kidDirection: Draw a dry path through the rain boot route office.
pages.adultNote: Let the child solve the route by drawing arrows before writing sentences.

sections.heading: Route Choices
lines: The hero changes the route by ____________________________.

pages.title: Tiny Forecast Cards
pages.kidDirection: Fill in four tiny forecast cards for Teacup Town.
pages.adultNote: Cut the cards apart or let the child number them in story order.

pages.title: Rain Gauge Railway Switches
pages.kidDirection: Match each railway switch to the garden spot that needs the rain sample.
pages.adultNote: Keep the focus on clear sequencing and simple cause-and-effect writing.

sections.heading: Switch Notes
lines: The hero checks the timetable because ____________________________.

pages.title: Snack Delivery Dialogue
pages.kidDirection: Write polite dockside dialogue that clears up a snack order.
pages.adultNote: Model one line aloud, then let the child complete the rest with short speech lines.

sections.heading: Dialogue Lines
lines: Ferry cook: "I can make it clearer by ____________________________."
Order taker: "Thank you, I will write ____________________________."

pages.title: Puddle Reflection Description
pages.kidDirection: Describe what the puddle mirror shows before the next delivery.
pages.adultNote: Ask for sensory details from the page, not a long paragraph.

sections.heading: Look Closely
lines: The reflection looks bright, dim, wavy, or clear: ____________________________.

pages.title: Weather Clue Sentence Builder
pages.kidDirection: Build three sentences from Teacup Town weather clues.
pages.adultNote: Point to one column at a time so the child can assemble sentences without guessing.

sections.heading: Choose an Action
lines: asks each shop for one clue

sections.heading: Choose a Detail
lines: because steam clouds look like commas.
when toast-scented fog fills the cup.
after drizzle taps the umbrella shop.

pages.title: Railway Weather Report
pages.kidDirection: Write a short weather report from the railway conductor's view.
pages.adultNote: Treat this as a four-sentence bridge between planning and the final story.

sections.heading: Report Notes
lines: The switch sends the sample to ____________________________.

pages.title: Snack Delivery Story Plan
pages.kidDirection: Plan the beginning, middle, and ending of a spoon ferry delivery.
pages.adultNote: Use this page if the child prefers lunchbox details over weather measurements.

sections.heading: Beginning
lines: The hero boards the spoon ferry with ____________________________.

sections.heading: Ending
lines: The menu card is fixed by ____________________________.

pages.title: Kind Ending Choice Cards
pages.kidDirection: Choose one ending card and add it to your story plan.
pages.adultNote: Offer two cards at a time if all four choices feel like too much.

sections.heading: Ending Card A
lines: The hero invites each shop to add one helpful clue.
Best for: Teacup Town Weather Window.

sections.heading: Ending Card B
lines: The hero maps the railway route with clearer labels.

sections.heading: Ending Card C
lines: The hero rewrites the menu so every cafe understands.
Best for: Spoon Ferry Lunchbox Harbor.

sections.heading: Ending Card D
lines: The hero copies the dry route onto leaf cards.
Best for: Rain Boot Route Rangers.

pages.title: Final Rainy Day Story
pages.kidDirection: Use your favorite planning page to write one complete rainy-day story.
pages.adultNote: Accept a short complete story and ask for only one revision pass.

sections.heading: Middle
lines: The route, order, forecast, or sample gets mixed up when ____________________________.

sections.heading: Ending
lines: The world is easier to understand because ____________________________.

pages.title: Bonus: Try the Quest Again
pages.kidDirection: Change one small detail and make a new mini quest.
pages.adultNote: Use this as an optional second-day page or a fast finisher station.

sections.heading: Mini Quest Cards
lines: Teacup Town: move one forecast card to a new pocket.
Rain Gauge Railway: send one sample to a different garden post.
Lunchbox Harbor: rewrite one menu word so it is clearer.
Rain Boot Rangers: copy one sliding path onto a leaf card.
